framework.text: The framework every Vanderbilt manager shares. Management is behavior, not a title, and behavior can be named, measured, and practiced. Vanderbilt uses Gary Yukl’s taxonomy of leadership behavior, published in 2012 in the Academy of Management Perspectives: four categories, fifteen behaviors, each category defined by the objective it serves. Category one, task-oriented: accomplish the work efficiently and reliably. Planning, clarifying, monitoring, problem solving. Example: goals written where the team can see them, and progress checked in the one-on-one before the deadline. Category two, relations-oriented: build the quality of the people and the relationships. Supporting, developing, recognizing, empowering. Example: praise that names the person and the act, within the week. Category three, change-oriented: increase innovation, collective learning, and adaptation. Advocating change, envisioning change, encouraging innovation, facilitating collective learning. Example: the why explained in your own words before the announcement, and a ten-minute debrief written down. Category four, external: get the team the information and resources it needs and defend its interests. Networking, external monitoring, representing. Example: knowing your HR partner by name before you need them. A good manager does all four. A great manager knows which one this week needs. The Managerial Practices Survey you will receive measures exactly these fifteen behaviors. Now tap each category on the page to open it, then turn the page for the first one.

task.text: Task-oriented behavior: get the work done well. In Yukl’s taxonomy this is category one of four, behaviors one to four of the fifteen the survey measures, and its objective is to accomplish the work efficiently and reliably. New managers skip it most, because they assume the team already knows what they know. The team does not. Behavior one, planning: before the quarter, three priorities, an owner for each, and a decision about what moves if a new request lands. Behavior two, clarifying: every person can say, without notes, what they own, by when, and what done well means; it is written in Culture Amp, not in your head. Behavior three, monitoring: you look at the work in progress in the weekly one-on-one, not the finished product on the due date. Behavior four, problem solving: when something breaks twice, you find the cause and change something, instead of fixing it a third time yourself. Watch for the difference. The habit is assuming, emailing the goal once, checking when it is late, and doing the work yourself. The Vanderbilt way is written, confirmed, checked weekly, and fixed at the cause. Now flip the four cards below, then turn the page and make your first call.

relations.text: Relations-oriented behavior: build the people. In Yukl’s taxonomy this is category two of four, behaviors five to eight of fifteen, and its objective is to build the quality of the people and the relationships the work runs on. It is where Vanderbilt’s engagement scores are made or lost. Behavior five, supporting: someone mentions a hard week at home; you listen, adjust what you can, and follow up on Monday. Know where support ends and a duty begins: a possible leave request goes to leave administration the same day, and you never ask for a diagnosis. Behavior six, developing: once a quarter, without a form in front of you, ask what each person wants to be doing in two years and find one stretch assignment to match. Behavior seven, recognizing: the way you handled the vendor call on Thursday kept us on schedule, said on Friday. Specific, named, within the week. Great job everyone names nobody. Behavior eight, empowering: hand over the decision, not only the task, and ask the team before you set a new process. Watch for the difference. Friendly is not supporting. The annual review is not developing. Now flip the four cards, then turn the page for a conversation that is half personal and half a leave request.

change.text: Change-oriented behavior: make the team better. In Yukl’s taxonomy this is category three of four, behaviors nine to twelve of fifteen, and its objective is to increase innovation, collective learning, and adaptation. It is how the Chancellor’s charge of speed, agility, and scale happens at the team level, one manager at a time. The detail most people miss: this is not reorganizations. Most of it is small and weekly. Behavior nine, advocating change: a new system is coming from central; explain the reason in your own words in Thursday’s team meeting, before Tuesday’s campus-wide email, and write down the objections to take back. Behavior ten, envisioning change: in two sentences, what your team will be able to do next year that it cannot do now. Behavior eleven, encouraging innovation: someone suggests a new way to run the weekly report; say, try it for two weeks and show me. Behavior twelve, facilitating collective learning: ten minutes after the event, what worked, what did not, what changes, written where the next person can find it. Watch for the difference. Forwarding the announcement is not advocating. That is not how we do it here is the opposite of innovation. Now flip the cards, then turn the page; the new system is coming and the team already hates it.

external.text: External behavior: connect the team. In Yukl’s taxonomy this is category four of four, behaviors thirteen to fifteen, and its objective is to get the team the information and resources it needs and to defend its interests. Every team depends on things it does not control, and at Vanderbilt that means dozens of business units, schools, and central offices, in more than one city. This is the category new managers most often do not know exists. Behavior thirteen, networking: know your HR partner, your Engagement Consultant, the person in Finance who approves your requisitions, and a peer manager in another unit, by name, before you need any of them. Behavior fourteen, external monitoring: read the compensation cycle calendar in August and tell the team in September what to expect in October, instead of learning about it from them. Behavior fifteen, representing: another unit’s request would break your team’s month; show the hours, name the collision, offer two options, and negotiate the deadline instead of absorbing it or refusing it. Watch for the difference. Meeting your HR partner at the first crisis is the habit. Names known before they are needed is the Vanderbilt way. Now flip the three cards, then turn the page and make the call on that request.
